extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and publishing rights/permissions staff (including in-house counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors and publishers on managing copyrights, obtaining and recording permissions, applying fair-use principles, handling fees and releases, and legal risk-avoidance when preparing material for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights database
rubrics_metrics.description: One prerequisite to an efficient and legally safe rights and permissions program is a complete and accurate record of what rights the publisher has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record third-party materials embedded in licensed material; record any other conditions restricting ability to license (for example, requirement that the author's approval be obtained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's copyright warranties
rubrics_metrics.description: In signing a contract the author warrants that the work is original, that the author owns it, that no part has been previously published, that no other agreement to publish it is outstanding, and that any copyrighted material of other authors used is used with permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless publisher otherwise agrees, burden falls on author to obtain permissions; indemnification backing these warranties is often negotiated. Publisher should not rely blindly on warranties and should be alert to exposures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other author warranties (defamation, privacy, accuracy, safety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should warrant that the work does not libel anyone or infringe privacy; may be asked to warrant that scientific formulas or practical advice will not cause injury; some publishers ask for warranty of factual accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher should query potentially risky material during editorial process; defamation defined as assertions of fact about living people that would likely hold the subject up to scorn or ridicule; invasion of privacy includes public disclosure of private facts that would be highly offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel versed in rights, permissions, defamation, and privacy can help review passages and determine whether permission is needed or a passage is defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel should have direct communication with author if appropriate (noting counsel represents publisher). Counsel's suggestions for manuscript changes should be followed absent compelling reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: permission required unless fair use
rubrics_metrics.description: An author must obtain permission to use any copyrighted material created by others, unless the intended use is a 'fair use'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permission need not be in writing technically but oral permission is unwise. No permission needed for US government works or public-domain works. Always credit sources as good practice and to avoid plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's role in obtaining permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing agreements generally place on the author the responsibility to request any permission needed for the use of material owned by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author should keep records of all copyright owners; begin requesting permissions as soon as manuscript accepted; obtaining many permissions may take weeks or months; many publishers decline to start typesetting until permissions are in hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview and photo releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain interviewee's permission for extracts that exceed fair use; obtain releases for photographs of living persons used on covers or in marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best to obtain broad release at time of interview (written or recorded). Using an image inside the book to illustrate text usually does not require a subject release, but cover/marketing use does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission to reuse author's prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Permission may be needed to reuse or revise an author's own previously published material if the prior publisher owns the copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain written permission or secure right of reuse in prior contract; credit prior publication as courtesy or if required by prior contract; flag files so future permissions requests refer to original copyright owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and record keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Most publishing agreements stipulate that any fees to be paid for permissions will be the author's responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When permissions are received, author should send copies to publisher; publisher will note and comply with any special provisions and will file permissions with the publishing contract; copyeditor will check permissions against manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissions beyond immediate use (scope limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissions may withhold sublicensing rights, limit licenses to a single edition, set maximum print runs, or limit to a specific time period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If limited, publisher receiving permission must go back to source for new permissions for new editions, reprints, serialization, etc., or negotiate upfront fees/automatic permissions for further uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissions for unpublished works
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtaining permission for unpublished material requires dealing with the author or heirs, who may be difficult to identify or find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start early; if author is dead it may be especially difficult to determine who controls copyrights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing copyright owner / orphan works
rubrics_metrics.description: When copyright owner cannot be located (orphan works), conduct a reasonable and well-documented search before using the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bona fide search may include Copyright Office records, internet searches, and queries to private/public databases. If owner later appears, be prepared to offer and pay a reasonable permissions fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-copyright restrictions on archives
rubrics_metrics.description: Private restrictions unrelated to copyright may limit use of archival/unpublished material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the collection's keeper (librarian/archivist) to learn what permissions are required; remember copyright in a manuscript is different from ownership of the physical paper—access and reproduction permissions may both be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use statutory factors
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining fair use, consider: (1) purpose and character of the use (commercial or nonprofit educational), (2) nature of the copyrighted work, (3) amount and substantiality of portion used, and (4) effect on potential market or value of the copyrighted work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four factors guide whether copying without permission is lawful; no exact boundaries are defined by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical guidance on invoking fair use
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors invoking fair use should transcribe accurately and give credit; should not quote so as to misrepresent original author's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformative uses (changing context or perception) are judged more leniently. Substantial quotation acceptable for critique but not acceptable to reiterate same argument; avoid quotations that overshadow quoter's own material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and the 'heart of the work'
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of quoted material matters more than absolute length; small percentages can infringe if they constitute the 'heart' of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never quote more than a few contiguous paragraphs or lines of poetry at a time; avoid quotations that substitute for or diminish the value of the original work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigraphs and interior monologues
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation as epigraph or within interior monologue does not fit neatly into usual fair-use categories but is probably fair use by scholarly and artistic tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not justify publishing a collection of epigraphs or lyrics without permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use of unpublished works — additional considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoting unpublished works, give some consideration to the interests of the author or the author's surviving relatives in controlling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same fair-use factors apply, but sensitivity to heirs' interests is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrasing treated as copying when extensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive paraphrase is traditionally treated as disguised copying; fair-use analysis applies similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small paraphrases may be so minimal they do not constitute copying; extensive paraphrase risks infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use for pictorial and graphic materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Fair-use analysis for images is uncertain; reproducing details for scholarly critique can be justified, but reproducing an entire image in vivid full-page color may compete with the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use minimal image size/quality necessary to convey historical context or illustrate analysis; cover or marketing use is usually commercial and requires stronger justification. See Code of Best Practices in Fair Use for the Visual Arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charts, tables, and graphs — special judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduction of charts, tables, and graphs requires judgment: some view a single item as equivalent to a few sentences; others argue a graph is a picture worth a thousand words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an item represents a small portion of both works, harm seems minimal. Simple data-presenting graphs/tables with little expressive input may be fair use or even uncopyrightable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Always identify the original source when reusing others' materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution bolsters fair-use claims and avoids plagiarism. Use clear legends like 'Reprinted from [author, title, date]' when material itself is copied; 'Source: [author]' is preferable when data are reformatted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary permissions; defend fair use when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Many publishers seek permission when doubtful, which can chill scholarship and slow publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requesting permission should not be seen as admission that permission is needed. If permission is denied or priced unreasonably, consider whether a sound fair-use case exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher fair-use guidelines (Chicago example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers can post generous fair-use guidelines for their own works to reduce expense and friction in permissions handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such guidelines (e.g., University of Chicago Press) are intended to be fair and are encouraged for adoption by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting permission — information required (identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permission requests should identify the title of the original work and exact identification of what is to be reprinted, including page numbers and, for prose, opening and closing phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tables/figures include figure/table number and page; be sure to cite the original source, not a subsequent reprinting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting permission — information required (publication details)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include information about the publication in which the material will appear: title, approximate page count, form (cloth, paperback, e-book, journal), publisher, probable date, approximate print run, and list price if available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing detailed publication data reduces delay and miscommunication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting permission — kind of rights requested
rubrics_metrics.description: State clearly the kind of rights requested: the most limited reasonable rights are 'nonexclusive world rights in the English language, for one edition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A better opening request is 'nonexclusive world rights in all languages and for all editions in print and other media, including the right to grant customary permissions requests but only where the licensed material is incorporated in [the requester's work].' Understand licensors may have their own forms and fee demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and record of permission requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Send permission requests in writing and in duplicate; retain copies of the final agreement with original signatures and provide copies to the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The copyright owner should state the fee and special conditions; both parties should retain final signed agreements; a third copy should go to the publisher's files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of model/sample permissions letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Using model request letters (on personal or institutional letterhead) helps define the request and facilitates replies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers (e.g., University of Chicago Press) can supply model letters to authors/editors who need to request many permissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digitizing and automating permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Photocopying and electronic reproduction have increased volume of license requests, prompting the use of online systems and standard fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properly designed websites and services (e.g., Copyright Clearance Center) can enable immediate permissions and predictable fees, increasing efficiency for publishers and users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations — rights holders and licensing realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Permission to reproduce pictorial works used as illustrations will rarely be available from the publisher; permission may be required from the owner of the object, the artist, or a museum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Museums may charge fees for providing reproductions or allowing photographs; although law may deny copyright to photos that merely reproduce two-dimensional images, publishers usually avoid antagonizing museums and comply with their requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock agencies and image archives
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs and pictorial works administered by stock agencies or image archives are typically easy to license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These agencies have clear inventories and fee structures; clearinghouse websites can make permissions straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information required for illustration permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Permission requests for illustrations should be specific about the identity of the image, the form of publication, and the kind of rights requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note any intended uses beyond the text (jacket, advertising) so licensors can price and condition permissions appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees for illustrations and scope of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees usually cover one-time use (first edition or certain number of copies); separate/higher fees are customary for jacket or advertising use and for subsequent editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should try to obtain permissions covering all editions and media; negotiation may determine who (author or publisher) pays for cover use or subsequent uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledging sources and credit lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether or not permission is required, an author should give the exact source of material via notes, source notes, or credit lines under illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow any special wording stipulated by grantor. Example acknowledgments: 'Reprinted by permission of the publisher.' or 'Courtesy of [institution]'. For reprinted materials prefer 'Reprinted from [author, title, date]'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgments sections for many permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: In works needing many permissions, acknowledgments are often grouped in a special section at front or back of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite grouping, some citation should still appear on the page containing the relevant material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for payment of permissions fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing agreements generally make the author responsible for fees charged for use of others' material, with some exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks often are exceptions where publisher may pay; publisher may agree to pay and deduct from royalties or split fees; authors should verify contractual terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthologies — early permissions work
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilations composed entirely of other authors' material depend on permissions from various copyright owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compilers should begin seeking permissions as soon as contract or letter of intent is in hand; until permissions and fees are agreed, table of contents cannot be considered final.
